title: Senior's toolkit: heaps and sorted collections
summary: PriorityQueue, SortedSet and SortedDictionary: the trees .NET gives you, what they cost, and the debugger views for recursive code.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: heaps and sorted collections
steps.body: You learned how heaps and search trees work so you can choose them well. In production code you use the framework's: a binary heap in `PriorityQueue`, and balanced red-black trees in `SortedSet` and `SortedDictionary`.

toolkit.what: A min-heap: the smallest priority comes out first. Enqueue and Dequeue are O(log n), Peek is O(1). Schedulers, Dijkstra, top-k, merging sorted streams.
flags: TryDequeue(out var item, out var priority)
enqueue again with the new priority and skip stale entries when they come out

toolkit.what: Push then pop the smallest in one O(log n) step. With a heap capped at k items it keeps the k largest of a huge stream in O(n log k) time and O(k) memory.
flags: add many at once; into an empty queue it builds the heap in O(n)
check the size to keep the heap at k
look at the contents, in no particular order

toolkit.what: A balanced binary search tree: unique items kept in order, O(log n) add, remove and contains, even when items arrive already sorted.
flags: the items in a range, inclusive
toolkit.example:
var free = new SortedSet<int>(slots);
var morning = free.GetViewBetween(9 * 60, 12 * 60);

toolkit.what: A dictionary that enumerates in key order. Tree-based: O(log n) insert and lookup. `SortedList<TKey, TValue>` is its array-based cousin: less memory, but O(n) inserts.
flags: built once, then read, or index by position
often simplest when you need order only once
toolkit.example:
var byDay = new SortedDictionary<DateOnly, decimal>();
foreach (var s in sales) byDay[s.Day] = byDay.GetValueOrDefault(s.Day) + s.Amount;

toolkit.what: For recursive tree code, stop at the interesting node and see every frame above it. Right-click a breakpoint to add a condition.
flags: one frame per level of recursion; double-click to see its locals
toolkit.example: Right-click the red dot > Conditions > node.Left == null && node.Value > 100

steps.explain: `PriorityQueue` is a min-heap: the smallest priority comes out first, whatever order items went in.
The set keeps items in order whatever order they were added. `GetViewBetween` includes both ends, so 40 is in.

steps.prompt: The nightly leaderboard job runs `scores.OrderByDescending(s => s.Points).Take(10)` over 50 million scores and now runs out of memory. What is the better approach?
options: A `PriorityQueue` capped at 10 items (min-heap on points, `EnqueueDequeue` once full): O(n log 10) time, memory for 10 items
Put all scores in a `SortedSet` and take the last 10
Run the query twice, once per half of the data
steps.explain: Sorting buffers every score to order them all, though only 10 are needed. A size-10 min-heap keeps the 10 best seen so far; the smallest of them is at the top, ready to be pushed out. A `SortedSet` also stores everything, and drops equal scores.

steps.prompt: A hand-written binary search tree is loaded with customer ids from a sorted export. Lookups become slow and a recursive `Insert` finally crashes with a stack overflow. What happened, and what do you use instead?
options: Sorted input builds a tree that is one long branch (height n), so every operation is O(n) and recursion is n deep. Use `SortedSet` or `SortedDictionary`, which rebalance
The tree has too many nodes; increase the thread's stack size
Ids must be inserted in descending order
Recursion is always wrong for trees
steps.explain: An unbalanced BST is only O(log n) on random input. The framework's red-black trees stay balanced whatever order the data arrives in.

items: Always run the job with the earliest deadline next
Keep the 100 slowest requests from a stream of millions
Free appointment slots, unique, asked for by time range
The smallest and largest active session ids
Daily totals that must print in date order
A price ladder from price to quantity, updated constantly

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: When you need "the next" or "the top k", reach for `PriorityQueue`; when you need order or ranges with frequent changes, `SortedSet` or `SortedDictionary`. When recursive code misbehaves, use a conditional breakpoint and the Call Stack window instead of printing every node.
